title: Medieval Lifting Wisdom
summary: NH looks at physical culture in the European Middle Ages: harsh conditions that made strength a requirement for survival, peasants and kings who exercised for fun and status, and knights as an elite trained by rucking and climbing in armor and hitting heavy objects. He argues that modern comfort has removed the incentive to be strong and calls for putting the body back at the center, as the basis for moral and masculine virtue.
claims: You can diagnose a culture's degeneration through its myths: when the heroes it worships are replaced by mediocre or degenerate idols, the population follows
Male power fantasy legends like the chansons de geste (Guillaume) still motivate young men 700-800 years later
Modern people have more knowledge only because information is easy to access in the digital era, not because they are smarter; they often lack wisdom
Medieval life was defined by discomfort and danger: about 35% of people died before age 20, and famine, cold and predators killed the weak
In the Middle Ages physical development was a prerequisite for survival, not a status symbol; today's comforts and support systems remove the incentive to be strong
Medieval peasants exercised for fun after work: running, jumping, wrestling and throwing rocks; you do not need fancy equipment to build your body, just the will
Medieval aristocrats trained through water sports and weapons practice
Children were pushed to become physically tough before cultivating the mind; NH wants physical education back, since 2 hours of PE a week is not enough
A strong, resilient body is the key to independence and brings unmatched confidence
Scholars back then worried about young men's vanity about their bodies (aesthetic bros existed in the 1500s); today the problem is reversed and most people cannot stand looking at their bodies
The average medieval man had the physical development of a dedicated modern gym rat
The low medieval median age of death is dragged down by infant and youth mortality; many adults lived into their 60s, 70s and 80s in good health
Medieval exercise mostly happened outdoors, in the sun and among trees, because people felt part of nature
Exercise is a break for the mind: alternate developing body and intellect until you die; the perfect man is both a beast and an intellectual
Strip away hobbies like Instagram, Netflix and porn and lifting becomes your favourite pleasure; make it your one hobby
Laziness breeds laziness and motion builds motion; desk workers who sit all day have the most reason to train after work
Medieval exercise was social (dances, organised wrestling) and strengthened community cohesion and the group's ability to defend itself
Women trained too, and children started physical development from about age 10
A study during lockdown found countryside children had about twice the arm strength of city children just from playing outside
Modern men's weakness and falling testosterone are cultural, not genetic; DNA does not devolve that fast
Discomfort breeds comfort and discipline brings freedom
People who call training vain miss the point: you train precisely because you are not perfect
Kings wrestled: François I reportedly tossed Henry VIII around; very few modern politicians are athletic
In 1369 a French king banned dice games in favour of physical activity
Becoming a knight meant years as page and squire, knighthood at 21 with at least 10 years of hard labour behind you; it conferred nobility and was originally a meritocracy that even accepted Saracens
Healthy cultures have rites of passage that turn boys into men; France abolished military service and now has none
Knights built endurance by walking, jogging and marching in 50-70 lb of armor, which developed back, legs and cardio; most modern people could not wear a 20 lb vest for long
Knights ate huge amounts of meat, cheese, fat and protein with few vegetables, thousands of kcal a day to match their expenditure
Descriptions of knights mention broad shoulders, big arms and legs, a thin waist, a developed chest and core, and a wide, thick back
Knights had to mount a horse in armor without help and trained one-arm variations: specificity and variation show that programming comes naturally to strong men
Knights struck heavy objects top to bottom all day, which built the upper back like wood chopping does
Knights went shirtless in the cold to show off their physiques; men's urge to display strength has never changed

Knights did weighted pull-ups by climbing ladders explosively in armor (salmon-ladder style), progressively overloading by adding armor pieces; also one-arm climbs, handstand push-ups and rock presses
Moral and spiritual degeneration follows a rotting body; put the body at the center of life
Building a big, strong natural body properly brings a philosophy with it; the journey teaches you
Healthy masculinity is great strength that is contained and put in service of others; the only shield against toxic masculinity is masculinity itself
Chivalric codes only make sense for strong men; imposed on weak modern men they turn into vices
Knighthood died when merit was replaced by lineage: once accomplishments stopped mattering, the incentive and the physical culture disappeared
Modern men still have the same masculine potential as their ancestors; it is the environment and their upbringing that shackle it
exercises: walk, hike or jog for long periods in 50-70 lb of armor
explosive two-hand climb in armor, controlled negative, add armor pieces to progress
weighted pull-up equivalent for big lats
pull yourself onto the horse with one arm in armor
specific strength, arm and back power
hit a large object top to bottom with an axe, stick or sword
builds the upper back like wood chopping
